pages.x: The emperor Justinian, ruling from Constantinople, had won back North Africa and much of Italy and built the great church of Hagia Sophia. In 541, with his armies still at war, a new sickness appeared at Pelusium, a port on the edge of Egypt.

In the spring of 542 the plague reached Constantinople, probably on the grain ships from Egypt. The historian Procopius, who lived through it, says that at its worst 10,000 people died in the city each day. The emperor himself caught it, and lived.
People would suddenly run a fever, and then swellings, buboes, rose in the groin and armpits. Many fell into a coma or raved; most died within days. No one knew it was spread by fleas from rats.
There were too few living to bury the dead. Procopius says great pits were dug, and when they were full, bodies were piled inside the towers of the city walls, until the whole city stank.
pages.of: deaths a day in the capital, said Procopius

pages.x: The plague spread to Italy, Gaul, Spain, Persia and Arabia, and came back again and again for two hundred years, until about 750. Farms lost their workers, taxes fell and armies shrank, just when Justinian needed them most.
In 2013 scientists found the DNA of the plague germ, Yersinia pestis, in skeletons from a graveyard of the 500s in Bavaria.
pages.fx: It proved that this plague was the same disease as the Black Death of 1347: the first of three great plague pandemics in history.

pages.x: The plague weakened both Rome and Persia just before the armies of Islam came out of Arabia, and some historians see it as the moment the ancient world turned into the Middle Ages. How many died is argued over: guesses run from a few million to tens of millions.
